chapter_theme: First songs at Palani (பழநி, 1 of 7): the poet confesses courtesans who sell love, take wealth and embrace without regard to caste, his begging from patrons, and a life run from birth through lust to the pyre, and asks for Murugan's feet, grace, the meaning of the mantra and the work of worship; the praise turns on Murugan as Siva's teacher, as the Tamil saint who defeated the Jains, as the all-pervading tradition, and on the goddess of Palani.
structure_note: Most follow the two halves. The confessions are of women (104, 108, 111 to 113, 117, 118), of a whole life (110, 115) or of household ties (109); 106 is a hymn to Murugan as what fills all things, 107 a short prayer for the guru's mantra, 114 a song on those who chant the six faces, and 116 an akam song for a lovesick girl.

104.reading: The poet calls himself a witless man who joins the followers of the six sects without shame and keeps friendship with women who give their favours for coins on beds scented with agil and musk, and asks when he will go to Palani and grasp Murugan's feet, worn with vetchi and kuravu flowers, which end the deeds of birth. The praise names him the one who, for the glory of Pugali, cured the fever of the Madurai king and sent the Jains with their grass mats to the stakes, who helped Nakkirar among poets against the horse-faced demoness, the son of Siva who burned the cities with a smile, and the one who wrote a poem and cast it on the water.
104.nuance: The praise makes Murugan the Tamil saint of Sirkazhi (புகலி) who cured the Pandya's fever with holy ash (பொடி) and impaled the Jains, the story told of Sambandar; the closing lines (கவிதை ... எழுதி வனத்தே எற்றிய) seem to recall the palm leaf thrown into the river in the same contest. துரகமுகக் கோதை and நக்கீரர் point to the story of the poet Nakkirar rescued from a horse-faced demoness. முப்பால் செப்பிய may name the Kural, but the phrase's syntax is not clear to me.

105.reading: The poet says that by the arrows of women's eyes and the flower arrows of Kama, son of Vishnu, he is struck with disease, loses his senses, wastes away and, taking on what Yama takes, dies, and asks for grace to leave the sea of births and reach the high good state. The praise names Murugan who took a seer's form and won the fruit of the hill, who imprisoned lotus-born Brahma over the meaning of the Pranava, and who, when Siva bowed and bowed again and praised him, told him the one word lovingly, at Palani with walls of coral, white and gold.
105.nuance: ப்ரணவத்து உரையைக் கருதிச் சிறைவைத்திடுவோனே and பணியப் பணியப் பரமர் பரவ ... ஒருசொல் பகர்வோனே tell the pilot's Om story in full: Brahma jailed for the meaning of Om, Siva bowing to receive one word. கணி நற் சொருபத்தை எடுத்து மலைக் கனியைக் கணியுற்றிடுவோனே is unclear; it may be Murugan taking a fortune-teller's form to win Valli.

106.reading: The poet describes Murugan as the one tradition that stands filling everything, the nether worlds, the earth, the gods' worlds, the cosmic egg, the seas, the eight directions, fire, sun and moon, the twilight mantras, the Veda, the tattvas and the atom within the atom, and says that Murugan came and first gave him the experience in which, as dark breaks at sunrise, the lotus of the heart opens; holding to sweet poems of crafted Tamil, will his rightful servant trust any world but him? The praise is a battle sung in drum syllables, with Kali dancing and foxes and vultures feeding, ending at Palani as lord of the gods.
106.nuance: The plea is unusual: no confession, only a grateful refusal to trust the world (ப்ரபஞ்சம்) after an experience already given (அநுபவம்). அணுவில் அணு, the atom within the atom, and the long list of worlds and elements make Murugan the all-pervading Lord, as Tirumular says of Siva. உரிய அடிமை is the poet's title for himself, service and not bondage.

107.reading: A short song: the poet asks whether, no longer wandering in harm and slander and no longer seeking out ignorant deceivers, he will think of Murugan through the meaning of the mantra of instruction and gain grace. The praise names him the younger brother of the elephant-faced god, the son of Himavan's excellent daughter, the true guru who gave the rosary, at Thiruvavinankudi.
107.nuance: உபதேச மந்திரப் பொருள் is the meaning of a mantra given by a guru, and ஜெபமாலை தந்த சற்குருநாதா makes Murugan the guru who gave the rosary; the song does not say to whom, but it reads like the poet's own initiation. Thiruvavinankudi is the shrine at the foot of the Palani hill.

108.reading: The poet describes courtesans at their toilet, bathing in turmeric and scent, dressing in many saris, combing and knotting their hair, setting their earrings, putting a camphor dot on the forehead, smearing agil and musk on their breasts, darkening their eyes for love's glances and wearing lily ear-flowers, then laughing so that young men and even ascetics weaken; he asks for Murugan's golden feet to end the desire and sorrow he has given to these women who take wealth. The praise names the vel that churned the sea of the Suras' blood so the gods survived, Murugan who wears the hunter girl's feet on his head and gives his shoulders to Devayanai, the peacock rider with the cock banner, at Palani.
108.nuance: The whole first half is the courtesan's preparation, step by step, and its end is பொருள்கவர் மாதர், women who take wealth. துறவினர் சோர claims that their laughter loosens even renouncers. குறமகள் பாதச் சேகர reverses rank as in 15: Murugan wears Valli's feet as a crown.

109.reading: The poet asks that instead of thinking real the wife who delights in a life of desire, the kin, those close to him, the children who please him, the rich land and the town he holds, he be given the work of praising and worshipping Murugan. The praise names him the tongue that spoke instruction into the ear of the lord who rides the bull, the head that bears the hunter girl's feet on her watch-platform, the twelve-shouldered one to whom Indra gave Devayanai, at Palani.
109.nuance: மெய் என மனம் நினைவது நினையாது: the fault is taking household and possessions for real, and the cure is a task, வழிபடு தொழில். Siva receiving instruction in his ear (செவிபுக உபதேசம்) is the Om story without the word Om.

110.reading: The poet traces his life from birth through crawling, walking, lisping speech and growing to sixteen, saying that he never praised the feet of devotees who recite the Siva texts, Agamas and Vedas but wandered in many cares with growing desire for women, and asks Murugan to join him to his feet. The praise names Siva who taught in silence and wears the moon, arugu and thumbai on his crown, the mountain's daughter who came as his half, and Murugan her son, the vel who walked on the peacock so the earth shook, the Murugan who is the supreme state, at Palani.
110.nuance: The omission confessed is not worship of the Lord but praise of his devotees' feet (அன்பர் திருவடிகளே நினைந்து). மவுன உபதேச சம்பு is Siva teaching in silence, the Dakshinamurti form.

111.reading: The poet describes women who learn a life without virtue, send cruel vel-like glances, put away a man's understanding, bargain a price, lay him on the bed, give the nectar of coral lips and hold his body tight with bangled arms, women like wax in the furnace, and asks for a release that ends the madness of love's play that melts him with them. The praise names Murugan whose chest the hunter girl embraced, whose fierce vel made the demon's hill melt and fall, and his mother, Rudri who loves drums, the dark-haired Shakti beside Siva, old Parvati, Kotri and Periyanayaki, at the great hill of Palani.
111.nuance: விலைபேசி, bargaining a price, marks the women as courtesans. மதன நாடக பித்து, the madness of Kama's drama, calls the affair a performance. The praise gives as many lines to the goddess as to Murugan, ending with பெரியநாயகி, a name of the goddess at Palani.

112.reading: The poet names the women's lively eyes, nectar speech, smile, drum-like waist, scented hair, deceitful young breasts and earrings, and asks for grace so that the trouble of ties with women who give an unfailing infatuation does not close round him. The praise names Murugan who killed Sura, who would not circle his feet or respect him and fought him, crying 'wait, wait, you will not escape', the son graced by the one whom Brahma and Vishnu could not know, the vel at Palani, lord of the gods.
112.nuance: The plea is built as a list of the women's charms, each ending ஆலே, 'by', and the danger is called சோரா மயல், infatuation that does not slacken. The meaning of ஆதாளிகள் and of புரிவரு in the last lines is not clear to me.

113.reading: The poet describes women whose eye-corners, keen as a killing vel and deadly as poison, rouse desire in young men, who swear oaths, hold them back, catch the men worth having, take all the wealth in their hands, then quarrel and bewilder them, and embrace without regard to caste; he asks for grace to leave their pleasures and, as Murugan's servant, praise and think of his feet daily. The praise names him the wonder given by the lord of Alavay who wears the moon, datura, erukku, arugu and pulai flowers, the nephew of Vishnu who shot the magic deer and pierced Vali's chest, the one who sought out the hunter girl in the forest Narada told of, and the lord holding the full-wisdom spear at Palani.
113.nuance: கைப்பொருள் மாள and சாதி பேதம் அறத் தழுவி: the women spend a man's wealth and embrace any man regardless of caste, the charge Parimelazhagar also makes on Kural 913. உனக்கு அடியான் sets the poet's service against his bondage to them. ஞான பூரண சத்தி names the vel as Shakti, full of wisdom.

114.reading: The poet speaks of devotees who chant 'Arumugam' six times with holy ash, take as their aid the feet of those who wear the feet of great ascetics, and say daily 'Guha who rides the peacock, Saravana, my lord, my honour is yours', and asks: if you only ask what these poor ones' trouble is, who will praise you, and what will the Veda not say? The praise names Murugan with a body like gold under ash, son of Uma, the lion-like vel thrown to end the poet's evil deeds, the companion of the elephant-faced god who took the life of the raging asura, at Palani, boon-giver to Brahma.
114.nuance: ஆறுமுகம் repeated six times opens the song with the chant itself. The question in the second quatrain seems to bind Murugan's fame to his care for devotees: if he neglects their distress, who will praise him? Its syntax (ஏழைகள் வியாகுலம் இது ஏது என வினாவில்) allows other readings.

115.reading: The poet tells a whole life: a human seed is born crying, crawls on the lap, toddles with dancing steps, runs in the streets, is taught the arts, at sixteen joins with young girls, weakens to Kama, sings poems in praise of patrons, runs to every quarter for wealth, melts in pleasure on scented beds and sinks in women's breasts until disease ruins his mind; then Yama chases him with the noose, parents and kin weep, they say Brahma's leaf has run out and carry him with drums to the burning ground, and those who embraced him bathe and leave the bond. Before that, he asks Murugan to come now and give the love that bows at his true lotus feet and melts singing Tamil poems. The praise, after drum syllables, names the vel that pierced the sea and split the seven hills, Murugan the guru-child of Uma, the nephew of Rama who felled Lanka's heads, who knew the Vedas and tested Tamil, at Palani, the lord who moves within his devotees' lives.
115.nuance: The cremation is told in detail (நவப்பறைகள் கொட்டா, சுடலை, சடம் பெரிது வேக), and the last act of the mourners, நீரில் படிந்து விடு பாசத்து அகன்று, is that they wash and let go. The leaf by which Brahma set the span of life (ஓலைப் பழம்படி) is the summons the pilot calls சமனோலை. The plea, இனி வரவேணும், is to come before this ending.

116.reading: Spoken for a girl sick with love: the moon climbs the sky like the sun, the submarine fire and poison, Kama shoots his arrows and the cuckoo calls, the drum of the seas, the flute and the bull's bell pierce her ears like iron, and women blame her; she cries 'Hara, Hara', longs for the peacock's rider and quarrels with everyone, and has grown faint. Though it is fate written on her head, the speaker says, taking her into his service is his burden; let him come on the horse that is Om to embrace her in her loneliness. The praise names Murugan the nephew of Krishna who kicked the cart, felled the twin trees and held up the hill against the rain, the son of the goddess under many names, the peacock hero whose vel turned the demon army to dust, and the delight of the hunter girl, at Palani.
116.nuance: The speaker calls her அகுதி இவள், this helpless one, so the voice is a mother's or friend's. அடிமைகொள உனது பரம், 'to take her as your servant is your charge', fuses the akam lover with the devotee. ஓகார பரி, the steed that is the syllable Om, is the peacock.

117.reading: The poet asks whether women's young breasts are two golden Merus, nectar pots, tender coconuts, elephant-hill peaks or the crown of Kama, says he fell into the maya of desire for them, praised as equal to the five heavenly trees men who never gave a coin, sang great Tamil and begged daily without finding a footing, and asks whether, trusting this diseased and ruined body and seeking life in vain, he will wander again in birth. The praise names his mother, Uma, sister of Vishnu and Kali who contended with Siva, the one who showed love to the Kaveri chieftain of Kalisai, the Kumaresa who came on the peacock so the asuras fell in the sea and Indra's heart was eased, and the lord whom the gods and Siva himself worship at Palani.
117.nuance: The confession joins two of the book's subjects, desire for women and begging from patrons in Tamil (ஒரு காசே கொடாதவரை ஐந்து தருவை நிகரே யாக ... புகழ்ந்து), and the begging is plainly in order to pay for the first. கலிசைவரு காவேரி சேவகன் seems to be a patron or devotee named in the praise; I cannot identify him.

118.reading: The poet describes women whose breasts are like caskets and hills, and the act with them, the hair loosened, the lips drunk, the embrace on the bed, the struggling and fondling, and asks whether he must wander so without any austerity. The praise names Murugan as the holy kinsman dear to Brahma, Vishnu's son, the one with the cock banner who fought the asura clan, and the one who lovingly told Siva the good meaning so he might know its fruit, at Palani.
118.nuance: தவமற்று உழல, wandering without tapas, is the whole plea. அரனுக்கு அருள் நற்பொருளைப் பகர்வோனே is the Om story without naming Om. அரிபுத்திர சித்த அஜனுக்கு ... மைத்துன வேளே makes Murugan Brahma's brother-in-law, perhaps because his consorts are counted Vishnu's daughters; the reading is uncertain.

links.note: Both follow the corpse to the burning ground with drums while the kin wail. The Naladiyar's drum mocks the man who still believes in household joy; 115 adds the mourners washing and letting go of the bond, and asks Murugan to come before that day.

Both say the paid embrace is false. The Kural likens it to embracing a stranger's corpse in the dark; 111 shows it from inside, the price bargained, the tight embrace and the man melting like wax, and calls it a madness from which only release frees him.

The Naladiyar says those set on the right path will not embrace such women; 108 says their laughter makes even renouncers weaken. If 108's துறவினர் சோர is taken literally, it doubts the Naladiyar's confidence; it may be only the poet's hyperbole.

Both speak for a girl sick with love for Murugan: the moon that burns like the sun, Kama's arrows and the blaming women torment her, and the speaker asks him to come to her. 101 asks for his garland, 116 for his embrace on the peacock that is Om.

Both confess begging from patrons by praising them in Tamil. In 15 the plea is to trade that service for service at Murugan's feet; in 117 the begging is tied to desire for women and to the ruined body, and the fear is another birth.
Both identify Murugan with the Tamil saint who sent the Jains to the stakes at Madurai; 104 adds the cure of the king's fever, holy ash and Pugali, the details of Sambandar's story.
Both run a life in one breath from infancy to youth and desire for women. 9 begins in the womb and ends in disease; 110 stops at sixteen and names the omission, never praising the devotees' feet.

Thiruppugazh 104 opens with the poet calling himself the witless one who keeps company, without shame, with the followers of the six sects (சட்சமயிகளொடு வெட்காது அட்கிடும் அறிவிலி), and turns to Murugan's feet at Palani. Tirumanthiram 1533 gives the reason such company is folly: those who saw the six sects did not see him, and he is not what they hold (ஆறு சமயப் பொருளும் அவனலன்). The song's self-reproach rests on the claim the Tirumanthiram states; the split of அட்கிடும் is not certain.

Thiruppugazh 105 asks for grace to leave the sea of births and reach the high good state (பிறவிக் கடல் விட்டு உயர் நற்கதியைப் பெறுதற்கு அருளைத் தரவேணும்). Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்). The song, beaten by Kama's arrows, asks for what the Kural names as the only crossing, and asks it of grace rather than of effort.

Thiruppugazh 106 makes Murugan the one tradition that fills the worlds, the elements and the tattvas down to the atom within the atom (அணுவில் அணு எனநிறைந்திட்டு நின்றது). Tirumanthiram 2008 calls the First Lord the atom within the atom (அணுவில் அணுவினை ஆதிப் பிரானை) and says only those who divide it a thousandfold can approach him. The same phrase serves the song as a sign of pervasion and the Tirumanthiram as a sign of subtlety to be approached.

Thiruppugazh 107 asks whether, through the meaning of the mantra of instruction (உபதேச மந்திரப் பொருளாலே), he will think of Murugan and gain grace, and names him the true guru who gave the rosary (ஜெபமாலை தந்த சற்குருநாதா). Tirumanthiram 2429 reports the gift as received: the Lord told him the mantra that cannot be spoken (உரைசெய்யா மந்திரம் சொன்னான்) and he stands wearing his feet. What the song asks for, the Tirumanthiram speaks of as done.

Thiruppugazh 108 spends its first half on the courtesan's toilet, turmeric bath, saris, combed hair, camphor dot, agil and musk paste on the breasts (அகில்புழுகு ஆரச் சேறு தனத்திட்டு), and asks for the feet to end the desire it rouses. Naladiyar 48 asks whether those who praise sandal paste and garlands (படுசாந்தும் கோதையும்) have not seen vultures tear the stinking cart once its axle breaks. The Naladiyar supplies the end of the body the song only adorns.

Thiruppugazh 109 asks that, instead of thinking real (மெய் என மனம் நினைவது) the wife, kin, children, rich land and town, he be given the work of worship. Kural 345 says that for those set on ending births even the body is excess, so what of other ties (மற்றும் தொடர்ப்பாடு எவன்கொல்). The song lets go of the household; the Kural extends the same letting go to the body itself.

Thiruppugazh 110 confesses that from birth to sixteen he never praised the feet of the devotees who recite the Siva texts, Agamas and Vedas (மறை ஓதும் அன்பர் திருவடிகளே நினைந்து துதியாமல்). Tirumanthiram 547 says the poet entered the Lord's city by going with the devotees of the Lord's devotees (உடையான் அடியார் அடியாருடன் போய்). What the song regrets omitting is, in the Tirumanthiram, the very way in.

Thiruppugazh 113 describes women who swear oaths, rouse desire and then make a man's wealth in hand run out (கைப்பொருள் மாள) before quarrelling and bewildering him. Naladiyar 377 says those who think theirs the love of a woman who licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from their hands (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு) and then turns away will be laughed at. Both name the same sequence, a show of love, the hand's wealth taken, then the turn.

Thiruppugazh 114 speaks of devotees who wear holy ash (பூதி) chanting Arumugam, take as their aid the feet of those who wear the feet of great ascetics, and say 'Guha who rides the peacock, my Lord' (ஏறுமயில் வாகன குகா ... எனது ஈச). Tirumanthiram 2111 says those who wear the ash crying 'you who ride the bull, our Lord, our master' (ஏறுடையாய் இறைவா எம்பிரான்) are devotees, and those who wear the feet have no deeds left. The two verses share the cry, the ash and the worn feet, with the mount changed from bull to peacock, and the song's vel that ends evil deeds matches the Tirumanthiram's வினையில்லை.

Thiruppugazh 115 follows a life to the pyre and ends with those who embraced him bathing in water and leaving the bond (நீரில் படிந்து விடு பாசத்து அகன்று). Tirumanthiram 145 ends the same way: they burn him, bathe in water and stop thinking of him (நீரினில் மூழ்கி நினைப்பொழிந்தார்களே). Both make the bath, not the burning, the moment the living let go.

Thiruppugazh 115 and 895 both tell the funeral rite by rite, drums, pyre and the mourners' bath, and both end the mourners' grief at the water (115: நீரில் படிந்து விடு பாசத்து அகன்று; 895: மருவு புனல் முழுகி மனை புக்குத் துக்கமறு). 895 adds that Kama then takes the mourners again, so the bath that ends grief begins desire; 115 instead asks Murugan to come before that ending.

In Thiruppugazh 116 the sounds of the night, the sea's drum, the flute and the bull's bell, pierce the lovesick girl's ears like an iron spike (வேயோசை ... இருசெவியின் நாராசம் உறுவதென). In Kural 1228 the herdsman's flute (ஆயன் குழல்) is the burning evening's messenger and a weapon that kills. Both turn the pastoral flute, sweet in itself, into a weapon against the separated woman.

Thiruppugazh 117 confesses that he praised as equal to the five heavenly trees men who never gave a single coin (ஒரு காசே கொடாதவரை ஐந்து தருவை நிகரே யாக) and begged daily in great Tamil without finding a footing. Kural 1067 begs all beggars not to beg of those who hide what they have (கரப்பார் இரவன்மின்). The song is the Kural's warning lived out: the poet begged of exactly those the Kural names, and found no footing.

Thiruppugazh 118 and 831 are near-repeats in the same metre: both open with breasts like a pair of caskets, round and thrilling (இருசெப்பென ... வட்டமும் ஒத்து இளகிப் புளகித்து), both ask whether, struggling and embracing (சருவிச் சருவி), he must wander without tapas (தவமற்று உழல), and both name Murugan the kinsman of Vishnu's son and the cock-bannered fighter of the asuras. The praise differs at the close: 118 has Murugan tell Siva the good meaning, 831 has him speak the three Tamils to those who love him.

source_issues: Song 106: line 20 runs two lines of the stanza together (அகில நிசிசரர் ... துங்ககாளி), breaking the stanza's layout.
Song 115: முழ்கி (line 12) should be மூழ்கி, and பிணியமுடிச் (line 12) and வாழவுக் (line 47) look garbled; none is flagged as corrupt.
